GATESVILLE.
Citizens Demand Punishment for Mob Violence.
GATESVILLE, Feb. 24. About two hundred citizens of Cowhouse came to town yesterday. Their mission wa to demand the arrest of the murderers of young Deering, who was taken by a mob from the officers and hung, in this county, a few days ago. Some of their party made affidavit, upon which Justice Hedgepeth issued a warrant. Sheriff Friend and posse left last night and about twelve o'clock to-day returned with Bob Divenett and two sons, who are now in jail. The trial is set for Tuesday. Other parties may be arrested. Still it rains.

Saturday Morning, Marth 4, 1882.
A few days ago a man named Bullet Deering was arrested by an officer in Coryell county for carrying a pistol and was tried before a magistrate and fined one hundred dollars and cost. Failing to pay the amount, he was ordered to be lodged in the Gatesville jail. Before reaching Gatesville it became necessary to stop and spend the night with Esquire King. During the night (which we learn was Monday night, the 13th inst.) a mob came Monday night, the 13th inst.) a mob took charge of Bullet and carried him about three hundred yards from the house and hung him until he was dead. We cannot think that the mob hung the man merely for carrying a pistol. Certainly they must have had some better excuse.—Belton Journal.

On the night of the 11th inst. Isham Edwards, a colored tenant on the Papy place, six miles from the city, on the Thomasville road, had about fifty panels of fence burned by malicious scoundrels. Mr. C. Harrison, of Columbia county, has cotton seven inches high growing in a patch, and about ready to bear forms.
The grading of the Peninsula Road is finished to Lake Panasoffkee.
Moses Sims, a colored man, in attempting to board a Chattahoochee steamer last week, was drowned. He resided in Jackson county.

The large saw mill at Boardman Station, near Hawthorne, on the Florida Southern Railway, and belonging to the owners of that road, was burned on the night of the 23d. Four flats loaded with lumber were destroyed. Loss, $15,000. The accident delayed the trains on the road several hours.

His father, who is a resident of Canada, is 116 years of age. He had an uncle, Davis Eaton, of Virginia, who died in 1822 at the age of 130, and who was a Mason 102 years of his life.

Swingley and Daniel Livingston, the parties employed to select and grade the Disston lands in this county, have selected and graded from township 50 to the Anclote river north, and from the Gulf coast to range 19 east, which includes all the northwestern part of this county, with the exception of one township and a few odd sections, on which they are now at work."

Tallahassee Floridian: "Captain C. A. Bryan has a strange but beautiful anomaly in his flower garden. A large rose bloomed on one of his bushes, and when the leaves began to fall from it four small but complete roses appeared in the centre, and now on the end of the stem where the large rose grew may be seen four fully-developed roses not larger than a gold dollar."

The wind was quite fresh at the time from the north, and the fire raged in a southerly direction, causing sad havoc to property among the people along its line. Messrs Bevan, Weedman, Cooper, Randall, Corbitt and others lost their fences, and Mr. Corbitt lost one hundred young orange trees. The inhabitants of the section through which the fire passed turned out in force to subdue the flames, and it is to their unwearied efforts that the residences along the line of the fire were saved."

Kreamer will occupy the position of General Superintendent of the Atlantic and Gulf Coast and Okeechobee Land Company. James M. leandel-hustled-maumee-1882-03.A1: Rape at South Toledo.—On Saturday last, a worthless wretch named Philan- der Husted, who lives in South Toledo, outraged a little 12-year-old girl, the daughter of Daniel Long, an old and de- crepid ex-soldier. The little girl visited Husted's house for milk, as she was in the habit of doing each day, and in the absence of the family of the worthless fiend the outrage was committed. Husted was arrested and locked up on Sun- day evening, and the excitement had become so great that it was thought he would be taken out and lynched. A rope was secured for this purpose, but cooler councils prevailed. Later in the day the wretch attempted to commit suicide by cutting a vein in his arm, but the at- tempt was discovered in time to save his life. He plead guilty at the preliminary examination on Tuesday.

OHIO STATE NEWS.

An effort is being made to enforce the Liquor Law at Akron.

Geo. A. BLACK, of Gambier, harness maker, has made an assignment.

At Moxahala Edward Downs was crushed to death by a moving elevator.

Mr. John Toomy attempted to board a moving freight train at Bellevue and was killed.

Frank Sullivan, of Wooster, was accidently drowned in the canal at Massillon. He leaves a family.

J. W. LACKENS, boot and shoe dealer, of Fostoria, has failed. Assets, $22,000; habilities, $24,000.

CARL MILLER, a brakeman on the Pan Handle Road, was knocked off his train by a bridge near Zanesville and killed.

WILLIAM SHIVES, who sued the town of Wooster for $1,000 damages sustained by the overflow of water, secured a verdict of $100.

NEWTON FILLEY, of Carbon Hill, was killed by a tree falling upon him while walking along the railroad track. He leaves a wife and three children.

ALLEN SETTLES, of Newark, is in durance vile for swearing that a fifteen-year-old girl was eighteen. Allen wanted to marry the young thing.

ANTON HOPP, German, aged fifty-seven, has been missing from his home at West Jefferson since December 27. A reward is offered for information concerning him.

W. J. LAMPTON, the well-known humorist of the position of city editor of the Louisville Courter Journal, beginning with March 1.

NORA MILLER, a thirteen-year-old girl, was probably fatally burned at Zanesville by her little sister setting fire to her dress with a lighted stick which she was playing with.

SMITH MILLER, a young school teacher near Mount Gilead, struck one of his scholars four licks with a base-ball bat, and at the Equire's request, paid therefor ten dollars per lick.

MISS CLARA HINTON, of Hallville, has sued Nelson E. Hall for $10,000 damages because he married another girl instead of providing her with a home. All the parties belong to the "upper crust."

BEACH WOODS, an old man of Unionville, attempted to chastise a grandson named Jimmie Poland, who, in return, hit the old gentleman on the head with an iron wedge and crushed his skull, injuring him fatally.

The Edison Telegraph Company, with a capital stock of $100,000, has been organized at Van Wert. It will extend, when completed, from Cincinnati to Hillsdale, Mich., along the line of the C., V., W. and M. Railroad.

A young lady, seventeen years of age, daughter of C. Sullivan, section watchman for the Columbus, Hocking Valley and Toledo Railroad Company, at Buchtel, was accidentally shot by an older brother fooling with a rusty revolver, resulting in a very dangerous wound in the groin.

M. Gilbert, a prominent farmer living near Cuyahoga Falls, signed a contract to become a book agent. The contract proved to be a promissory note for $350, which Gilbert paid the sharper rather than stand suit. All he got for his money was a $1.50 sample bible.

EAST GREENVILLE, five miles west of Massillon, is without a postoffice. The Government would pay but $60 for carrying the mail to that point, and the Postmaster being unable to secure any one to perform the services for that amount, was left without an occupation and hence gently resigned.

CHARLES JONES, aged twenty-one years, is in jail at Richwood on the charge of having two wives, to which he pleads guilty. Some time ago Jones married Miss Brachus, of Knightstown, Indiana, and after living with her a short time, returned to Richwood and married Miss Johff, Mrs. Jones No. 1, hearing of this marriage, went to Richwood and swore out a warrant for the young man's arrest.

JACOB WHITMORE has been convicted by a jury at Bellefontaine of murder in the first degree. His crime was that of poisoning his fourteen-year-old wife with strychnin in the woods on the 15th of September last. The jury were just one hour in finding a verdict. When the verdict was announced Whitmore broke completely down, fell over a chair and began crying like a child. He had evidently expected to be acquitted.

A HORRIBLE story comes from Maumee, in the northern part of the State. Leander Husted, a young man, went to the house of a neighbor, named Long, and finding the family absent with the exception of Nancy, aged eleven years, he outraged her in the most brutal manner. As soon as the parents learned the true state of affairs, Husted was arrested and placed in jail. So indignant were the people that they collected at the jail to lynch the friend, who, hearing their clamor, opened an artery in his arm, and before the authorities were aware of his condition, he had bled nearly to death, but prompt action saved him.

At Dandridge on Saturday the citizens by vote elected to have the town incorporated.

In Meigs county the farmers are making arrangements for the crop season. The acreage of peas, cotton, potatoes and oats will, no doubt, be largely increased; corn will fall back. Winter oats are looking well, and though the wheat looks well, yet farmers fear the show at this season does not promise well for a good crop.

A policeman shot at a fleeing negro in Nashville on Tuesday, but fortunately for both the officer and the suspected person the bullet missed its mark. Had the officer killed the fleeing negro he would have laid himself liable to prosecution for murder, inasmuch as it has been decided by the courts that an officer has no right to fire at an escaping person, unless he be a felon.

In the time of Governor Porter there was a large surplus in the State treasury, which he applied toward the payment of six months interest on the State debt. With this precedent before him, and a still larger sum in the treasury, it is possible that Governor Hawkins may direct the same disposition of it. Indeed, with nearly $2,000,000 in the treasury, what else can he do with it?

Chattanooga Times: "Grass is green and bright in all portions of the city and is growing rapidly.... There is a great demand for houses in the city at present. There are but very few to be had.... Cotton took another tumble yesterday and March futures fell fourteen points. Several dealers failed to make good their margins and in consequence there were some losses. We learn of one individual who lost $200."

Knoxville Tribune: "There are about ten candidates for justice of the peace of this district already.... Parkham Adams, a youth of fourteen, who is a student in the university at Knoxville, from Brownsville, on Saturday last undertook to smoke for a wager and stopped, much overcome, at his fortieth cigar. He then went to the skating-rink and had a bad fall from dizziness. He was taken home to his boardinghouse and next day had brain fever, and lay very sick from the effects of the nicotine, with small chances of recovery."

MALTBY, of Wilson, writes under date of the 2d inst., that as he reached Ellsworth that night his attention was called to the ceremony of hanging a man to a telegraph pole. w-e-graham-ellsworth-1882-01-02.A15:
JUDGE LYNCH AT ELLSWORTH.
ELLSWORTH KAN. Jan 3, 188
ELLsworth, KAN., Jan. 3, 1881.
EDITOR JOURNAL: I have twenty minutes in which to write you the eventful happenings of this city in the last 24 hours. When I arrived here this morning at 10 o'clock about the first thing I saw after the man who shouted, "Right this way for the Grand Central Hotel," was a man hanging from a telegraph pole with a rope around his neck. Upon inquiry I found he was Wm. Graham, who murdered his uncle and set fire to his shanty, in the northwest part of this county, about 5 days ago. All for $125. He was confined in the jail here, and had confessed his crime.

Monday evening, at 9 o'clock, a party of masked horsemen rode rapidly and quietly into town, hitched their horses at a convenient point and made a determined break for the jail. There they were met by Sheriff Stebins, who was powerless in the hands of an infuriated and determined party, as they were. The work of denolishing doors and Iron cells was a matter of slight hindrance to them, and they soon had in their power the confessed murderer. They took him at a rapid rate to the nearest telegraph pole—about 300 yards distance—placed a ladder to the pole and a rope around his neck, and bade him climb. He did as directed, and when on the fourth round of the ladder he swung off into eternity.

The active parties engaged were perhaps 25. It was generally understood during the afternoon that something of the kind would occur during the night. There were 300 witnesses to the tragedy.

After the vigilantes were satisfied he was dead, dead, they went back to the jail to get Mr. Rose, whom you remember committed a double...burden in the southeast part of the county in October, and who was confined in a cell adjoining Graham. But the officers had made good use of the time in getting him away before they re-appeared.

Graham's remains lie in the jail. The jury summoned in the post mortem examination rendered a verdict in accordance with the evidence, I suppose, or at least as they understood it. It was, "The deceased came to his death from strangulation, in part from his own exertion, and by the hands of parties unknown." This can the more readily be appreciated when it is known that his arms were pinioned behind him and the laadder placed nearly perpendicular. For this reason citizens are divided in their opinion about its being suicide or strangulation in part from his own exertion and by the hands of parties unknown.

Yours, B.

THE Atlanta exposition closed after a successful existence of three months.

W. E. GRAHAM, who killed, robbed and burned Philip Egley, at Venango, Kansas, on the night of December 28, was hanged by a crowd in front of the court-house the other night.

IN Missouri a child seven years old, having quarreled with a playmate aged five, obtained a revolver and shot his little adversary, killing him instantly.

WHILE attempting to escape from jail at Graham, Texas, three brothers named McDonald, charged with murder, were shot and killed, as was also a deputy sheriff. The McDonalds first killed the deputy sheriff and then broke out of jail and took another deputy sheriff along in their flight, compelling him to act as a shield between them and their pursuers. Then a pitched battle took place between pursuers and pursued, during which the McDonalds were all killed and three other men were wounded.

SAMUEL BECKLEY died at Flint, Mich., a few days ago, at the age of 109.

CLEMENT C. CLAY, formerly United States Senator from Alabama, died at his residence near Huntsville, Ala., age sixty-three years.

The Maryland legislature met at Annapolis and organized by the election of George H. Williams as president of the senate, and Otis Keilhoz speaker of the house.

THREE men employed on the Paradise tunnel ten miles from Silverton, Col., were buried one hundred feet deep in a snow-slide.

The prisoners in the jail at Hillsboro, N. C., overpowered the jailer and eight of them made their escape.

DURING the funeral of the pastor of the Salem Evangelical church, at Quincy, Ill., a panic was created by the giving way of a railing, and in the rush which followed for the doors about forty persons were injured, some so severely that recovery is doubtful.

At Catlettsburg, Ky., three men charged with the recent atrocious murder of the Gibbons children and Miss Thomas, were put on board a steamboat for conveyance to Maysville, the justices fearing that they would be lynched. A crowd obtained another steamer and pursued the sheriff's party until they heard that militia were coming, when they gave up the pursuit.

A NUMBER of men assembled in a store at Westport, La., quarreled about a horse race; revolvers were drawn, and in the general fight which followed three men were killed outright, a fourth was mortally wounded and two others were slightly hurt.

At Oskaloosa, Iowa, three boys—John Phillips, son of the mayor, Gerald Joyce and John Stedman—were shooting with rifles, using the side of a wooden building containing 500 kegs of powder as a target, when a terrible explosion occurred. The three boys were instantly killed, and their bodies, frightfully mangled and burned, were hurled from fifty to two hundred yards away. Nearly all the plate-glass windows in the vicinity were broken by the concussion, and many houses in the southern part of the city were badly damaged. Many persons were injured by the falling glass and debris. The shock of the explosion was felt at Monroe, a distance of thirty miles.

APACHE Indians attacked a mine in Arizona and murdered six men.

Three inmates of the Mason county (Ill.) poorhouse perished in the fire which consumed that institution.

Five men were hanged the other day—three in Missouri and two in Louisiana. At St. Louis, Joseph M. Kotovsky and Charles Ellis—the first white and the other colored—were hanged, Kotovsky for murdering a pretty servant girl who had rejected his advances, and Ellis for killing Mack Sanders, a patron of his gambling house. At Marshall, Mo., John A. Phelps was legally strangled for the murder of Elijah Keyton, a wealthy farmer, and at Frankin, La., Sterling Ben and Terence Achille, both colored, met their death on the gallows for killing D. Larmand, a wealthy citizen.

PETER MARKINS died the other day in Washington county, Ark., aged 111 years.

The total net decrease in the national debt during the calendar year 1881 was $133,690.018.90.

The official reports of the Guiteau trial make 1,775 printed pages, and with the arguments the full report of the trial will make a volume of over 2,000 pages. The cost to the government for this item alone will be about $5,000.

Some interesting correspondence has been made public concerning the case of General Fitz John Porter, who in January, 1863, was tried by court marshal and sentenced "to be cashiered and forever disqualified from holding any office of trust or profit under the government of the United States." In 1878 a board of army officers made a thorough examination in General Porter's case, and reported to the President that General Porter was guiltless of the charges preferred against him in 1863, and that the findings and sentence of the court marshal should be set aside and the accused officer be restored to his rank in the army. The correspondence now made public is a letter from General Porter to President Arthur, requesting that action be taken in his case; also a letter from General Grant to the President in which the general says: "At the request of General Fitz John Porter, I have recently reviewed his trial and the testimony furnished before the Schofield court of inquiry held in 1879, giving to the subject three full days of careful reading and consideration, and much thought in the intervening time. The reading of the whole of this record has thoroughly convinced me that for these nineteen years I have been doing a gallant and efficient soldier a very great injustice in thought and sometimes in speech. I feel it incumbent upon me now to do whatever lies in my power to remove from him and from his family the stain upon his good name." General Grant then asks the President to give General Porter's case early consideration. Another letter is published from General Terry to General Porter. In this letter Terry says he wronged Porter for many years and asks for pardon. The charge upon which General Porter was tried in 1863 was for neglecting to go to General Pope's assistance at the second battle of Bull Run.

Mr. Scoville is reported to have accepted an offer of $1,000 for Guiteau's body, the money to be paid at once and the buyer assuming the chances of the assassin's execution.

The President has transmitted to the Senate letters from Postmaster-General James and Mr. George Bliss, of counsel in the star route cases, accompanying a report of Postoffice Inspectors Tidball and Shallcross. This report shows an extended combination for defrauding the government by means of worthless bonds, and that its members have been able to impose on the postoffice department such bonds to the amount of $8,000,000 or $10,000,000.

The requisitions for stamps from postmasters at the postoffice department on the 7th aggregated over $640,000. This is the largest issue in one day in the history of the service.

The Huntingdon Journal says: Congressman Fisher wants a new Mint in Philadelphia. The putting up of new buildings at public expense is a cheap way of gaining notoriety—cheap for Mr. Fisher, but not for the public—and the notoriety, when obtained, will hardly last as long as it will take to build Huntingdon's Reformatory.

Edward Hines wrote to the Liverpool Mercury, "I am willing to risk my reputation as a public man, if the worst case of small-pox cannot be cured in three days simply by the use of cream of tartar. One ounce of cream of tartar dissolved in one pint of water drank at intervals when cold is a certain, never-failing remedy. It has cured thousands, never leaves a mark, never causes blindness and avoids tedious lingering."

The Huntingdon Local News says that on Wednesday evening, Anna, aged sixteen months, daughter of John and May Smith, of Huntingdon, swallowed a number of morphine pellets which she found upon a table. Shortly afterwards she was noticed to become stupid, and then it was discovered that she had taken the morphine. Dr. Brumbaugh, who happened to be passing the house, was called in and administered strong coffee and other antidotes, and the life of the child was saved.

The Newport News says: A recent dispatch from Ellsworth, Kansas, states that W. E. Graham killed, robbed and burned Philip Egly, at Venango, Ellsworth county, and was subsequently hung by a mob in front of the court house. Graham was the son of Isaac Graham, a blacksmith by trade, who moved from Newport to Millerstown last spring. Egly was also formerly from Newport, having emigrated to the west a year or so ago. According to the information received Egly had obtained some money by the sale of his property, and to get it Graham murdered and then set the house on fire to cover up his tracks. Egly was Graham's uncle.

On the 10th inst., W. Cloyd Guss, division foreman on the railroad, with residence at Black Log station, three miles north of this place, was run over by the cars and killed. The distressing event took place about noon. Mr. Guss had partaken of his dinner and gone out, and was only about 100 yards from the house when he was struck by a passing freight train. He had stepped out of the way of a train coming east on the south track into the way of a train going west on the north track. His wife was the first person to see him after the accident. She was looking out of the window and saw an object of the appearance of a man lie by the track. Quickly she sent a neighbor to the place. The neighbor returned with the painful intelligence that it was her husband. Dr. Banks was called, and examined the body of the unfortunate man. Both thighs were broken; the skull was broken, and the left leg was nearly severed from the body. Instant death was the result of the stroke from the train. Mr. Guss leaves a wife and two children to mourn his death. He was about 40 years of age. His remains were interred on Thursday, the 12th inst., in the Licking Creek Lutheran graveyard.

A Young Man Abducted from a Saloon and Not Seen Since.
ATCHISON, KAN., March 13.—The facts about the mysterious disappearance of Walter Saunders, a popular young citizen of Atchison, have been given by John Kennedy, an eye-witness of the abduction. Saunders was addicted to drink, and lost his position for indulgence in this habit. He went to Kansas city to clerk in a prominent boot and shoe-store there. Last Monday he, Edward Toller, book-keeper for Fowler Brothers, of Kansas city, and others, were drinking in a saloon, when four men rushed into the place, grabbed Saunders and forcibly dragged him from his friends. He was hurried up a dark alley by the party, now increased to twelve. His friends pursued and found that the mob had taken Saunders to a house, and there, in the presence of a thirteen-year-old girl named Flanagan, accused him of assaulting her. Saunders made no reply to the charge. He was then taken to the street and hurried in the direction of the Kaw bridge, and as he has never been heard from since it is supposed that he was thrown into the river. This supposition is strengthened by the fact that Ellet, one of two brothers strung up in order to force him to tell what had become of the missing man, said that he turned his back when they made away with him.

News of the Week.
John D. Dwyer, a well-known pugilist, died last week in a hospital in Brooklyn, of consumption.

The Secretary of the Treasury on Tuesday issued three calls for $15,000,000 of continued sixes, as announced previously.

Mormon missionaries are at work in the King's Mountain District of North Carolina, and have made about fifty converts to date.

Vennor gives notice that a severe wind storm, with heavy rain, will sweep along the Atlantic coast on the 18th and 19th instants.

A movement is on foot in Newport, Rhode Island, to procure the appointment of George T. Downing, colored, as Minister to Liberia.

John H. Bailey, tax collector of West Chester, Pa., was arrested in Philadelphia on Monday, charged with being short in his accounts.

Miss Armainda, who was to ride a bicycle 600 miles at St. Louis in six days, of 12 hours each, ended the ride Tuesday night, making 617½ miles in 51 hours 36 minutes actual riding time.

Robert McMahon, while having a frozen toe amputated, at Lindsay, Ont., on Monday, was put under the influence of chloroform. At the conclusion of the operation he was found to be dead.

H. G. Reese, serving a sentence of three years in the Auburn, N. Y., penitentiary for bigamy, committed suicide on Monday by hanging himself in his cell. He was formerly a clergyman.

The attorney General for the Post-office Department decides that toll gate and ferry keepers cannot lawfully detain the United States mails even if the mail carrier refuses to pay charges.

The American Print Works at Fall River, Massachusetts, have shut down for several weeks to curtail production. Similar action is being taken by other print works throughout the country.

A boat containing three sailors of the Australian bark Bulwark, arrived at Empire City, Oregon, on Monday evening, and reported the probable loss of the vessel with the rest of the officers and crew, 18 in all.

In a saloon at Syracuse, New York, on Sunday morning, Charles Smith challenged Henry Lentz to a fight. They went outside the saloon, when Lentz seized Smith by the throat and choked him to death.

Mr. J. C. Campbell, a merchant and planter, of Hampton, S. C., was thrown from his buggy and killed Saturday. He was tried the previous day on the charge of assault and battery with intent to kill, and appitted.

A crowd surrounded a barn in Scranton, on Sunday, for the purpose of lynching Daniel Wagner, 55 years of age, who had feloniously assaulted a little girl. He was arrested, however, and committed in default of $1000 bail.

In the United States District Court at Philadelphia on Monday, John Pasco, of Camden, N. J., was sentenced to eleven months imprisonment in the Eastern penitentiary for making a fraudulent application for a pension.

The President on Tuesday sent to the Senate a communication from the National Board of Health, calling attention to the necessity for additional legislation to prevent the introduction of infectious diseases from foreign countries.

Services were disturbed by a drunken man in the Lutheran church at Black River, Wis. The minister walked coolly down from the platform, seized the offender, threw him outdoors, and resumed his sermon as though nothing had happened.

The Secretary of the Interior has given permission to the Indian Agent at the Crow Agency in Montana to send one hundred of the children under his care to Ohio, to be bound to certain farmers to be educated and reared up in usefulness.

Mrs. Sarah E. Howe, president of the swindling concern in Boston known as the "Ladies' Deposit," was sentenced on Monday to three years' imprisonment in the House of Correction. She has already been eighteen months in jail.

A riot occurred in Third Creek, North Carolina, on Saturday, between about one hundred whites and blacks, growing out of a fight between one of each color. Troops quelled the disturbance, and many of the rioters were arrested and lodged in jail.

On Monday night some scoundrels cut the rubber tubes connecting with the air-brakes on 86 cars lying in the yards of the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul, Chicago and Alton and Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Companies at Chicago.

The county commissioners of Lancaster county, Pa., have offered a reward of $500 for the arrest of James Shaw, who murdered his wife on March 7, near Bartville, in that county. He is supposed to be in Philadelphia or Baltimore, and will probably try to escape to Ireland.
Jonathan Holmes Cobb, well-known as a lawyer and in connection with his successful but unremunerative experiment in 1826 to manufacture silk by the cultivation of large mulberry orchards in Massachusetts and in Virginia, died at Boston on Sunday, aged 83 years.

In the Senate of Massachusetts on Tuesday a resolution in favor of biennial state elections was passed by a vote of 26 to 7. In the House a prohibitory liquor bill was passed to a third reading by a vote of 105 to 80. It is similar to the old prohibitory law of Massachusetts, with the exception of a clause providing for its submission to the people.

A girl at Pekin, Ill., was about to be married to a young sweetheart. A man in the neighborhood heard of it, and told her mother that, as his wife was going to die soon, he would marry the girl himself, if she would wait. As he was rich, the bargain was made, and in three months the wedding took place.

On Sunday evening a mob of the railroad strikers at Omaha surrounded the quarters of the soldiers, and some brickbats were thrown at the officers. A squad of soldiers charged the moll, and a man named G. P. Armstrong received a bayonet wound in the breast, from which he died later in the night. The non-strikers resumed work Monday, and no further disturbances are reported.

Dr. James Still, colored, residing at Medford, Burlington county, N. J., died on Friday morning of last week at the age of 70 years. Dr. Still was known throughout the country as the "black cancer doctor," and was reputed to have made many wonderful cures. He was wealthy, and had erected a large hotel to accommodate his patients.

A great fan, which has for some time been in course of construction for clearing the railroad tunnel in St. Louis of smoke from passing trains, is now in successful operation. It is said that the entire tunnel can be cleared of smoke from the heaviest freight train in three minutes, and when no trains are in it the air is as clear and fresh as that outside.

The Fashionable Exodus to Europe this year will be very great. The inquiry for state rooms at the offices of the favorite lines in New York is said by the steamship men to be larger than ever. At the offices of two of the lines it was stated that applications for berths are fully double what they were two years ago. The demand has been such that there are but few berths left in the May sailings, and several of the steamers to sail in that month are now entirely engaged. The outgoing steamships Saturday carried nearly three hundred cabin passengers.

Walter Saunders, a clerk in a shoe store at Kansas City, Mo., somewhat addicted to drinking, while standing with a couple of friends in a saloon, a few days since, was seized by four men, who rushed into the building and dragged him outside, where they were joined by eight more. The whole party ran off, carrying Saunders with them. It is now said that he was taken to a house where a young lady charged him with assaulting her, and then his captors took him to the river and threw him in. He has not been seen by his friends since the day of his abduction.
